title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
description: Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.On Thursday, he arrived i
body: Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances. He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September. Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing. These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party. Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, says she is "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict."Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC. Human Rights Watch described the ruling as "cruel and unjust"."To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years, also for colluding with foreign forces.Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow, an activist who is now also in exile.But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader"."We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them... Instead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong.Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature – but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong."Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."Additional reporting by Martin Yip

schema.headline: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years

title: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
description: A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.The wom
body: A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.The women - identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 -were reported missing on 1 November when they did not return from what was supposed to be a short afternoon walk, the family said. Their remains were found in a trail area in Bella Coola, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS), which said evidence at the scene "suggested an animal may have been involved".Conservation officers are working to track down any bears involved. Balcarras' remains were found on Monday and Reed's on Tuesday during search efforts by conservation officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BCCOS, said it was not yet clear if more than one was potentially involved in the women's deaths. He added that any captured bear would be assessed and if it is found to have been involved in the attack "it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety". Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh Balcarras, told CBC."When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and begin a new chapter in her life, according to an online fundraiser to help the family with funeral costs.Grizzly bears are listed as a species of "special concern" under federal legislation, and are an important part of the British Columbia landscape, according to Environmental Reporting BC, external.Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in the province, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, which has classified them as vulnerable. According to the ministry, conflicts between bears and humans are "relatively rare" unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs and food. But there have been a number of attacks in British Columbia in recent years. A grizzly bear injured two hikers in the McGregor Mountain area in October 2025, one of whom died later due to critical injuries. The bear was later found dead. The following month, a bear attacked a school group - also in the Bella Coola area - injuring 11 people.The BC Wildlife Federation (BCWF) has said that reports of grizzly-human conflicts have risen since the province introduced a ban on hunting grizzly bears for sport in 2017."With no hunting pressure, grizzlies and humans will increasingly occupy the same spaces with inevitable consequences," the BCWF's executive director Jesse Zeman said at the time.

schema.headline: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada

title: Hungary opens secret police files, 37 years after fall of communism
description: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itsel
body: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule. Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members. The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution."I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity,"  Prime Minister Péter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest."Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer. Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided. Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary. Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.Krisztian Ungváry, a historian who has long campaigned for full public access to the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power."In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party. Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

schema.headline: Hungary opens secret police files, 37 years after fall of communism

title: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock
description: In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knes
body: In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem."In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said."One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening."In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared"."I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

schema.headline: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock

title: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life'
description: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.Ten
body: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally"."These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement."I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened."I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing."Rest in peace, Jesus."Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone."In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player."As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell"."Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

schema.headline: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life'

title: El Nino is making the Pacific 'burn with fever', triggering typhoon after typhoon in East Asia
description: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fishermen return to sea under a crimson s
body:
Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon DolphinByJoel GuintoBBC NewsReporting fromSingaporeKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Darren BettLead weather presenterWild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
                    
                        Typhoon Champi hit Taiwan and Japan
                    
                    
                        Source: NASA
                    
                El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.Image source, VCG via Getty ImagesImage caption, This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm NarraAugust brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.'Burning with fever'The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.Image source, ReutersImage caption, China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies'Very, very scary' simulationsIn August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people. They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.Figure caption, Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rainsPreparing for the onslaughtCountries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently."How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock."Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

schema.headline: El Nino is making the Pacific 'burn with fever', triggering typhoon after typhoon in East Asia

title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night
description: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentDemocrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map o
body: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentDemocrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map on a night that will send shockwaves through American politics for years to come.With a string of major Senate victories in states that have been reliably Republican for decades - and in Kansas's case, nearly a century - a blue tidal wave crashed across the nation, sweeping Republicans out of power.Halfway through President Donald Trump's second term, the Democrats now have decisive control of the House of Representatives and have wrested a majority back in the Senate. They will be able to frustrate Trump's agenda, and launch investigations into his administration. A historic third impeachment attempt could also be on the cards.Few imagined such an outcome was possible in the months after Trump returned to the White House with unified Republican control of Congress in January 2025. As the public mood turned against him and his party, Democrats had hopes of retaking the House.But they contemplated a Senate map that appeared unfriendly, populated by states Trump had won comfortably just two years ago.Instead, Democrats rewrote the political equations with victories in Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina.In comments to the BBC's US partner CBS, Trump pledged to strike deals with congressional Democrats, adding that he didn't want to have to spend his final two years in office rejecting their legislation.He somewhat undermined that sentiment later, posting a picture to Truth Social of his trademark red baseball hat with the word "veto" emblazoned on it.The president went on to note that his name wasn't on the ballot this year, but if it had been Republicans would have won a decisive victory. Trump had helped elevate many of those Republican candidates, however, and had urged voters to pretend he was up for re-election.LIVE: Follow latest updatesREACTION: Trump accepts Democrats did a 'good job' in electionTHE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key resultsGUIDE: What are the US midterms?In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least six seats, comfortably securing a majority.Adam Hamilton won in Kansas - a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate almost 100 years ago during the Great Depression.James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race, ending a 38-year Democratic losing streak in statewide elections there.In South Carolina, Annie Andrews beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. Few analysts had that seat in play even a few months ago.Five-term Republican Susan Collins conceded Maine's Senate election to Democrat Troy Jackson.Paralympian Josh Turek flipped the Iowa Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Democrats also wrested from Republicans a Senate seat in Ohio, with Sherrod Brown's comeback victory over Jon Husted.Meanwhile, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has beaten Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly fought Senate race.Nor was that the end of the electoral carnage for Republicans. Ruby-red Texas witnessed another seismic result in the governor's race.Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, who was earlier this year seen as the prohibitive favourite.Democrats also took governors' races in Iowa, Ohio and Georgia, which made history by electing the first black woman to such a post.Meanwhile, the party has won a House majority for the first time since 2022.They are projected to win 245 House seats and the Republicans 166 seats.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democrats celebrate in Maine where the party won a crucial Senate raceA look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.Democrats flipped House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Kentucky and Colorado, among others. And they were poised to make gains in Virginia and Indiana. Black Democrats in the southern states turned out in record number, helping to carry their party to victory. And Hispanic voters, whose support had helped secure Trump's presidential victory in 2024, swung decisively back to the Democrats.Democrats won all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border. And Hispanic voters helped Democrats hold House seats in Florida that the state's Republicans had sought to flip by redrawing the congressional district lines.In fact, the congressional redistricting battles that had dominated headlines for months last year ended up being a bust for the Republicans. In Texas, they had hoped their line-drawing would net five new seats for their party. But on Tuesday they may end up losing one seat.If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds, who was elected the Sunshine State's first black governor. And embattled Republicans were able to hold governorships in Vermont and New Hampshire. But the bright spots were few and far between.Just two years ago, Trump won the presidency with 48% of the vote. He claimed an electoral mandate. He then went about governing like it, pushing sometimes unpopular policies on trade and immigration, and launching an Iran war that is opposed by most of the American public.On Tuesday, voters gave him the kind of stinging rebuke that will not be easily forgotten.Figure caption, BBC asks voters across US what brought them to the polls todayFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night

title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
description: French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.T
body: French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies. "No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers. By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted."The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them."Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe."We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens."Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too."Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing."To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC. "Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.But no formal attribution has been made.None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats. Additional reporting from Chris Vallance

title: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'
description: Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans voted "NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stu
body: Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans voted "NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stunning defeat in the midterm elections."We endorse this message," parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X."If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he warned.Trump acknowledged on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in petrol prices. But he insisted that he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran in February.In an interview with Fox News, Trump said of the midterm results: "I think a part of it was Iran".He went on to say: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."Speaking separately to the BBC's US news partner, CBS News, Trump said the conflict would end "when I say it ends".In recent weeks, Trump has warned that the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei - who has not been seen in public since he was reportedly seriously wounded in the same Israeli air strike on the first day of the war that killed his father and predecessor, Ali - said he did not expect US policy to change. Khamenei released a statement saying anyone who thought there would be any change from American "hostility towards the Iranian nation" was "gravely mistaken". He also said the war would have "much wider dimensions" if it resumed.In a separate development on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.The IRGC said two of the vessels were still burning, and two additional tankers had been intercepted, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. It said they were trying to travel through a prohibited southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.BBC Verify has been investigating the IRGC claims, and has not found any evidence that four tankers were destroyed. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said a tanker was struck by two unknown projectiles about 14 nautical miles (26km) north-east of Limah, in Oman's Musandam peninsula, on Tuesday evening. No casualties were reported, it added.On Monday, an Indian crew member of a dhow - a wooden sailing boat - was killed in an attack north-east of Limah. Thirteen other crew members were rescued by Omani authorities.The IRCG also reported on Wednesday that its forces had shot down another US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.It made a similar claim on Monday night, when US officials said the US military had carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.In an interview with the Financial Times ahead of the midterms, Trump suggested he was happy with the state of the conflict, and that he did not consider them to be "really in a war".When asked about what the newspaper described as "strong hints" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack on Iran this week, Trump said they were "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".Indirect talks to end the conflict have been stalled for months.President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained on Tuesday that his government had been trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue"."No-one will benefit from this war" if it were to resume, he warned.He also emphasised that Iran's supreme leader had granted the government powers to negotiate "issues that he had previously considered off-limits".Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqai said on Monday that the basis of the current indirect negotiations mediated by Qatar remained a seven-step proposal that Iran submitted in September. But he added that the proposal had been "condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days".The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the Strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Additional reporting by Gabriela Pomeroy

title: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
description: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukr
body: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.Severely damaged buildings are also seen.A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha."Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops. Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians. "First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.The Russian military has not publicly commented.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.In a separate development on Wednesday, Zelensky said he talked "in great detail for an hour-and-a-half" with US President Donald Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US on 10-11 November in Abu-Dhabi.The Ukrainian leader - who is currently making a surprise visit to Spain - also said his team had a separate "meaningful" meeting in Brussels with representatives from the US, the EU, France, Britain, Germany, as well as Nato and the World Bank about "post-war reconstruction".He added that the meeting in Belgium's capital would continue on Thursday to discuss "security guarantees" for Ukraine.Since the trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.Analysts expect no major breakthrough when the talks resume in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.  Additional reporting Paul Brown, BBC Verify

title: Rafael Nadal: Tennis legend set to join Real Madrid board of directors
description: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and
body: Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and helped Spain claim five Davis Cups before retiring in 2024.Real's members will be asked to approve the 40-year-old's appointment to the board at a meeting later this month.In a statement announcing the move, external, the club said Nadal was "one of the greatest legends in the history of sport and one of the most admired and recognised Spanish athletes in the world"."It is a great source of pride that a figure of his sporting and human stature, a benchmark of Spanish and world sport, will become part of our board of directors and contribute, from this position of responsibility, to the present and future of our club," Real added.The tennis legend - a boyhood Real fan who holds member's number 67,778 - included a photo of himself as a child in a club kit in his response to the news."I want to thank president Florentino Perez and the board for proposing that I join the board of directors of Real Madrid," Nadal said in his post on X, external."I have accepted this proposal with great excitement, a desire to learn, and a willingness to contribute everything I can."It is currently unclear as to what responsibilities Nadal would hold on the club's board.Perez was re-elected to serve a new four-year term as Real president in June, having held the office since 2009.He swiftly appointed Jose Mourinho to a second spell as head coach, hoping to improve the club's fortunes after they went a second season without a trophy in La Liga, the Champions League or the Copa del Rey.Real are currently third in the league after 11 games - three points behind defending champions Barcelona.

title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
description: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 43 minutes agoVice-President JD Vance sent sho
body: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 43 minutes agoVice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election."The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington.  While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.Figure caption, Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake."If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.Image source, ReutersDrawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan:  "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

title: What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress
description: Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats w
body: Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory."Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, declared. After months of promises on the campaign trail — to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war —  they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.The Democrats should not consider what just happened "a mandate," US Senator Chris Coons told the BBC, warning that the party was still "deeply unpopular"."We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular."Congressman Robert Garcia of California will soon lead a powerful oversight committee in the House, with the power to make Trump's last two years in office quite difficult."Lawyer up," the Democrat said in a statement as victorious results poured in on election night.Committees in both the US Senate and House have investigative powers, which they could use to delve into alleged conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him. On Tuesday, Garcia rattled off a list of possible targets: Trump's family, "corporate corruption", alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the government's handling of the Epstein files.The Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. Should a US Supreme Court vacancy, for example, arise during Trump's term, Senate Democrats could use their new power to block a nomination - or force Trump to choose a more moderate candidate who garners bipartisan support.The House also has the power to impeach a president - the first step of Congress' process to remove an official from office.Democrats twice impeached Trump during his first term, though the US Senate eventually voted to acquit him in both cases. But because it takes a two-thirds majority in the US Senate — or 67 votes — convicting a president in an impeachment case likely will remain out of reach for Democrats.There's an active debate among Democrats about whether impeachment is a good idea. The first impeachment, in 2019, unleashed partisan rancor and allowed Trump to cast himself later as a victim of political persecution, which later helped build support for his second White House run.  Jeffries, who would almost certainly have to greenlight any Democratic impeachment effort, has kept his plans vague."Well, we've made clear: We haven't ruled anything in," he told CNN in August. "And we haven't ruled anything out".Americans' frustration with Congress' productivity was palpable before the election. Only 14% of US registered voters approved of lawmakers' performance, an October Gallup poll suggested.But with a Republican in the White House and Democrats running Congress, Americans may face even more deadlock."If you thought legislating was hard in the last Congress with unified Republican control, that will get much more complicated," said Casey Burgat, professor of legislative affairs at George Washington University.Because they will control both chambers with a comfortable majority, Democrats will be able to pass legislation through Congress with relative ease.Getting it enacted into law will be harder.A president must sign most legislation in order for it to become law. Trump has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress that he does not support, and Congress can only override him with a supermajority from both chambers - margins Democrats alone will not have despite their success on Tuesday. As his party lost Senate race after Senate race Tuesday night, Trump struck a conciliatory tone with the New York Times."We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," he said.But a few minutes later, Trump posted a picture on Truth Social of his red campaign hat with the word "VETO" emblazoned across the front. That Jekyll-and-Hyde approach to a Democratic Congress could become a theme.While opposition to Trump led to Democrats' success, lawmakers acknowledged Tuesday night, it might not be enough."It is overwhelmingly a rejection of Donald Trump, and his agenda and policies," Coons told the BBC."But if we overreach, or if we fight too much internally, we could miss this moment."Despite the veto threat, Jeffries has said that his party wants to restore significant cuts Republicans made to healthcare programmes like Medicaid, which is used by low-income groups, and the Obamacare marketplace."We're committed as a top priority as House democrats to reversing these Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits," Jeffries said at a September event for healthcare workers.On typically bipartisan issues – such as policies affecting affordability, regulating the AI industry, re-evaluating military funding for Israel and reining in the Iran War – talks could break down as lawmakers try to compromise. As they become the opposition heading into the 2028 presidential cycle, Republicans might not be in the mood to help Democrats achieve too many wins.Fissures also could erupt even among Democrats themselves, particularly on matters involving Israel, that may make party consensus difficult. A schism emerged in the Democratic Party during the midterms over continued US military funds for Israel.Incoming senators like Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, and some incoming members of the US House, said during the campaign they would vote for legislation to curtail aid to Israel. These Democrats could face a road block from their own leadership.Then there's the matter of reining in Trump's foreign policy, which could be difficult, despite Democrats' majority.Even before the midterms, Congress saw bipartisan efforts to limit Trump's ability to continue the war with Iran. Though some of these measures passed one or both chambers, Congress has not been able to enforce them. Notably, both the House and the Senate passed a resolution in June to halt hostilities with Iran, which Trump could not veto but has essentially ignored.The White House has argued Trump has broad powers to continue the war. But Congress' authority to force Trump's hand is an "open legal question," said Scott Anderson, senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution."Congress can try to litigate this out, and force the courts to tell us."

schema.headline: What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

title: Abdul El-Sayed, Melat Kiros, Adrian Boafo: The politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
description: "JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.Abdul El-Sayed,
body: "JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations."My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests. Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House. Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

schema.headline: Abdul El-Sayed, Melat Kiros, Adrian Boafo: The politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms

title: Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections
description: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByJames FitzGerald and Nardine SaadReporting fromLos AngelesDemocrats have won
body: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByJames FitzGerald and Nardine SaadReporting fromLos AngelesDemocrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.Projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans some reasons to commiserate. Here is everything you need to know about some of the big Democratic wins and some historic firsts.Democrats toast victories in deep-red Trump countryImage source, ReutersImage caption, James Talarico, the new US senator in Texas, and Gina Hinojosa, the state's new governor, toast their successesTrump congratulates opposition and acknowledges Iran and fuel prices were issuesTrump spoke throughout the evening to a number of US media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Congress. Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."He acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has impacted consumer prices in the US, had affected the vote. Trump argued that high fuel prices meant voters could not see how well his economy was doing "as much as they should have", adding: "The gasoline was caused by Iran."El-Sayed wins US Senate race in Michigan after fellow Democrat turns on himAbdul El-Sayed has become the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate - after claiming victory in Michigan in what was one of a handful of closely fought contests. His win means the seat stays in Democratic hands. He defeated Republican opponent Mike Rogers, who received the surprise backing of El-Sayed's Democratic rival in the primary contest, Haley Stevens, who changed her endorsement at the eleventh hour.The race was one of the bitterest of the midterms. Trump invoked 9/11 and even called El-Sayed a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.Image source, ReutersImage caption, El-Sayed triumphed in one of the bitterest contests of the midtermsEl-Sayed's supporters went wild when he took the stage to celebrate his claimed victory, wrote the BBC's Nada Tawfik. He said: "Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say 'inshallah,' or 'God willing,' whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned." He went on to say: "But today, tonight, we can turn that 'inshallah' into 'alhamdulillah'. For the right-wing ops, that just means 'praise be to God.'"Republicans unable to win by distancing from TrumpThe defeat of Susan Collins, who has served as the Republican senator for Maine for three decades, was one indicator of the scale of the Republican losses. She was felled by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, a logger who sought to point to his background to persuade blue-collar Mainers to vote for him.In a statement reported by US media, Collins conceded defeat and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve the state for 30 years. The BBC's Helena Humphrey described a sombre atmosphere at Collins's watch party in the city of Maine - where the song Closing Time was played.Image source, ReutersImage caption, There was a sombre atmosphere at the watch party for Republican Susan CollinsCollins entered the race as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election, and found that her tactic to distance herself from Trump did not work.Ashley Hinson suffered the same fate in Iowa, losing that closely-fought Senate seat to Josh Turek. Hinson had slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.History made by new black governors, first openly gay male senator and first Gen Z congresswomanAmong the other firsts of the night were in Florida, where Republican Byron Donalds has become the state's first black governor, following a hearty endorsement from Trump. Donalds, who will take over the job from Ron DeSantis, said his state was the "envy of the nation", and that he would work to make the state more affordable.The result was one of the few high points of an otherwise difficult evening for the Republicans. Image source, ReutersImage caption, A win for Bryon Donalds in Florida was one of the few high points for RepublicansIn the neighbouring state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, won the governor's race, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue. Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive. The state has also not had a Democratic governor for more than 20 years.Elsewhere, Democrat Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.Pappas defeated former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race, whom he thanked on Tuesday, saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."Figure caption, Watch: "I am ready to fight" - Senator-elect Chris Pappas celebrates New Hampshire winIn Colorado, Melat Kiros became the first woman elected to Congress from Gen Z - meaning those who were born between 1997 and 2012.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.
